segments.title: Why the T.2 Dart suited carrier decks
segments.body: The unusually large, single-seat Dart combined subtle, manageable handling with a wing loading of only nine pounds per square foot. Its stalling speed was 38 knots, which helped pilots land it on carrier decks. From 1928, aircraft received Handley Page slots as they came up for reconditioning. The slots made the Dart still easier to land aboard a carrier.

evidence.note: The Dart's gentle handling, low wing loading, 38-knot stalling speed, and Handley Page slots suited carrier-deck landings.

segments.summary: The Blackburn T.2 Dart paired gentle low-speed handling with deck-landing features that made a large single-seat aircraft workable aboard carriers.

segments.title: How the Dart helped refine aerial-torpedo technique
segments.body: The Dart remained in service for ten years despite its modest performance. Its rugged dependability helped the Fleet Air Arm develop and perfect torpedo-dropping techniques.

evidence.note: Despite modest performance, the Dart gave ten years of dependable service and helped develop Fleet Air Arm torpedo-dropping techniques.

segments.summary: The Dart's ten years of rugged service gave the Fleet Air Arm a dependable aircraft for refining torpedo-dropping technique.

segments.title: Dart torpedo training at Gosport
segments.body: D Torpedo Training Flight at Gosport used Darts to teach naval pilots how to approach a target for a torpedo attack. Pilots flattened out 15 feet above the water and aimed the whole aircraft at the target. These training aircraft were an exception to the Dart's usual employment at sea. Most Darts normally served aboard aircraft carriers, which gave the public few opportunities to see them.

evidence.note: D Torpedo Training Flight at Gosport taught 15-foot-low attack approaches in Darts, although most of the type served aboard carriers.

segments.summary: At Gosport, a Dart-equipped torpedo training flight taught naval pilots the close-to-the-water approach needed for an attack run.

segments.title: The Dart at public air displays
segments.body: Dart N9549, coded 1, appeared at the Hendon RAF display on 30 June 1923. On 10 November that year, another Dart carried a dummy torpedo at a Croydon display organized for Dominion premiers. Newly built N9689 was exhibited at Prague's Palace of Industry during the Third International Aero Show from 31 May to 9 June 1924. Five Darts from HMS Furious staged a mock torpedo attack on the dummy enemy ship Slavic at Hendon on 20 June 1924 before thousands of spectators. N9549 led the formation again, this time coded 4 rather than 1. These displays gave the public a rare view of a type that normally served aboard carriers.

evidence.note: Darts appeared at Hendon, Croydon, and Prague before five aircraft from HMS Furious staged a 1924 mock torpedo attack on the dummy ship Slavic at Hendon.

segments.summary: Four appearances in 1923 and 1924 gave the public rare views of a carrier-borne torpedo aircraft, ending with five Darts from HMS Furious attacking a dummy ship at Hendon.
